lede: A rope that pulls at an angle is doing two jobs at once: dragging along the floor and lifting. Resolving splits one slanted force into those two straight ones, so the rest of the mechanics can be done a direction at a time.
can: Split a force at an angle into a component along a line and one at right angles to it
Resolve the weight of a body on a slope into its two components
Read which angle to use, and which line it is measured from

caption: One slanted pull replaced by two at right angles.

md: Drop a dashed line from the tip of the force onto the line you care about. The force becomes the longest side of a right-angled triangle, and the two shorter sides are its components: the side beside the angle takes the cosine, the side opposite it takes the sine.

Two quick checks catch most slips. Each component is smaller than the force, and squaring the two, adding and taking the square root gives the force back. The larger component always goes with the smaller angle, so a large angle to the floor means a small part along it.

stem: A rope pulls a box with 46 N at 22° above the floor. Find the parts of the pull along the floor and straight up.

steps.decision: The floor is beside the 22° angle, so this part takes the cosine.
Straight up is opposite the angle, so this part takes the sine.

title: Mechanics FM GCSE - Resolving Forces on Horizontal plane
why: Taught straight against this specification. Watch the angle being marked on the diagram before either ratio is chosen.

prompt: A rope pulls a sledge with a force of 25 N at 40° to the ground. What is the part of the pull along the ground, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
explain: The ground is beside the $40°$ angle, so it takes the cosine, as step 1 of See it did: $25\cos 40° = 19.15$ N. The sine would give the part lifting the sledge.

twin.prompt: A rope pulls a cart with 34 N at 35° to the ground. What is the part of the pull along the ground, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: Beside the angle, so the cosine: $34\cos 35° = 27.85$ N.

text: Why cosine goes with the angle

title: Why cosine shortens the force
md: Think of the arrow's shadow on the line. When the force lies along the line there is no tilt, $\cos 0° = 1$, and the whole force counts. Turn it to a right angle and the shadow vanishes. Cosine is the fraction of the force that survives the turn.

stem: A force of 50 N is turned away from a straight line. How much of it acts along the line at $0°$, at $60°$ and at $90°$?

steps.decision: Lying along the line, the whole force counts.
Turned through 60°, half of it survives.
At a right angle to the line, none of it acts along the line.

prompt: A force of 20 N acts at 60° to a straight line. What is its component along that line, in newtons?
explain: Half the force survives a turn of $60°$, as step 2 of See it showed: $20\cos 60° = 20 \times 0.5 = 10$ N.

twin.prompt: A force of 44 N acts at 60° to a straight line. What is its component along that line, in newtons?
twin.explain: $44\cos 60° = 44 \times 0.5 = 22$ N: half of it survives a 60° turn.

caption: The weight split down the slope and into it.

md: On a slope the useful directions are along the surface and at right angles to it, so the weight is the force to split. The angle between the weight and the line into the slope is the slope's own angle $\alpha$: into the slope is $mg\cos\alpha$ and down the slope is $mg\sin\alpha$.

On any slope under 45° the larger part of the weight presses into the surface. Resolving the mass instead of the weight gives a number ten times too small: a component of a mass means nothing, so work out $mg$ first.

stem: A box of mass 11 kg rests on a slope inclined at 30°. Resolve its weight down the slope and into it.

steps.decision: Resolve a force, never a mass: the weight first.
Down the slope is opposite the slope's angle, so it takes the sine.
Into the slope sits beside the angle, so it takes the cosine.

prompt: A box of weight $W$ sits on a slope at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal. Which expression is the part of its weight pulling it down the slope?
explain: The slope's angle sits between the weight and the line into the surface, so the cosine part goes into the slope and the sine part runs down it, as in step 2 of See it.

twin.prompt: A crate of weight 80 N rests on a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Which is the component of its weight down the slope?
twin.explain: Down the slope is opposite the slope's angle, so it takes the sine: $80\sin 30° = 40$ N. The cosine gives the part into the slope.

optionNotes.why: That is 80 cos 30°, the part pressing into the slope; down the slope is opposite the slope's angle, so it takes the sine.
That is 80 tan 30°; a component of the weight is the weight times a sine or a cosine, never a tangent.
That is the part pressing into the slope, which sits beside the slope's angle; down the slope is opposite it, so it takes the sine.
Tangent compares the two components with each other; each component itself is the weight times a sine or a cosine.

caption: The angle is given to the vertical, not to the horizontal.

md: A question may give the angle to the horizontal or to the vertical. Whichever line the angle is measured from, the component along that line takes the cosine and the one at right angles to it takes the sine. So with an angle to the vertical, the vertical part is the cosine.

Look for the words 'to the horizontal' or 'to the vertical', and mark the angle on the diagram before choosing a ratio. Summer 2024 Q3 set forces with their angles given from different lines, and reading one from the wrong line cost marks.

stem: A force of 18 N acts at 25° to the vertical. Find its vertical and horizontal components.

steps.decision: The vertical is the line the angle is measured from, so it is beside the angle: cosine.
The horizontal is at right angles to the vertical, opposite the angle: sine.

prompt: A force of P newtons acts at 30° to the vertical. Which expression gives its vertical component?
explain: Measured from the vertical, the vertical side is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine, as step 1 of See it did.

twin.prompt: A strut pushes with a force of $Q$ newtons at 50° to the horizontal. Which expression gives its vertical component?
twin.explain: The angle is measured from the horizontal, so the vertical part is opposite it: the sine. The cosine gives the horizontal part.

optionNotes.why: That is the horizontal part, beside the angle to the horizontal; the vertical part is opposite it, so it takes the sine.
Tangent is the ratio of the two components, not a component of the force.
Measured from the vertical, the vertical side is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine; the sine gives the horizontal part.
Tangent is the ratio of the two components, not a component of the force.

prompt: A cable pulls with 30 N at 35° to the vertical. What is its horizontal component, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
explain: The angle is to the vertical, so the horizontal part is opposite it and takes the sine, as step 2 of See it did: $30\sin 35° = 17.21$ N. The cosine would give the vertical part.

twin.prompt: A strut pushes with 26 N at 50° to the vertical. What is its horizontal component, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: Opposite the angle to the vertical, so the sine: $26\sin 50° = 19.92$ N.

caption: Two pulls whose horizontal parts face each other.

md: A component has a direction as well as a size. Choose one way along the line as positive; a component pointing the other way is then negative, and it is subtracted rather than added.
Write the sign with the component as you work it out, and say which way is positive at the start of the line, so the total is a sum of signed parts.

stem: A point is pulled by 36 N to the right and by 14 N up and to the left at 60° to the horizontal. Find the total component to the right.

steps.decision: Beside the angle to the horizontal, so the cosine; it points left.

steps.working: Right positive: it counts as $-7$ N
steps.decision: Pointing the negative way, it is subtracted.
Not 36 + 7: the two parts face each other.

prompt: A force of 16 N acts at 60° above the horizontal, to the left. Taking to the right as positive, which is its horizontal component?
explain: Its size is $16\cos 60° = 8$ N, and it points left, the negative way, as the 14 N pull did in step 2 of See it: $-8$ N.

twin.prompt: A force of 22 N acts at 60° above the horizontal, to the left. Taking to the right as positive, which is its horizontal component?
twin.explain: Its size is $22\cos 60° = 11$ N, beside the angle to the horizontal, and it points left, the negative way: $-11$ N.

optionNotes.why: The size is right, but the force points left, the negative way, so its component carries a minus sign.
That is 22 sin 60°, the vertical part; the horizontal part is beside the 60° angle to the horizontal, so it takes the cosine.
The size is right, but the force points left, the negative way, so its component carries a minus sign.
That is 16 sin 60°, the vertical part; the horizontal part is beside the 60° angle to the horizontal, so it takes the cosine.

md: **A mass, not a weight** (2023, 2025). The question gives the mass; the weight $mg$ is what gets resolved. **Inside a longer question** (2019, 2022, 2024): the component is one line inside 'Calculate the normal reaction' or 'Calculate the value of $P$', and the first mark is for writing it down.

title: Not on this paper
md: A pull at an angle to a slope is not set. The Teacher Guidance puts every force applied to a body on a slope along the slope, so on a slope only the weight needs resolving.

stem: A parcel of mass 3 kg rests on a slope inclined at 30°. Find the component of its weight down the slope.

steps.decision: The mass becomes a weight before anything is resolved.
Opposite the slope's angle, so the sine.

prompt: A 12 kg crate is on a slope at 30° to the horizontal. How big is the part of its weight down the slope, in newtons?
explain: Weight first, as step 1 of See it did: $12 \times 10 = 120$ N. Then $120\sin 30° = 60$ N down the slope; resolving the mass would give 6.

twin.prompt: A 7 kg sack is on a slope at 30° to the horizontal. How big is the part of its weight down the slope, in newtons?

md:
Split any force into a component along a line and one at right angles to it.
Resolve the weight on a slope into mg sine and mg cosine of the slope's angle.
Read whether the angle is given to the horizontal or to the vertical, and choose the ratio.
Combine components that point opposite ways by subtracting.

Resolving is rarely asked for on its own: it sits inside 'Calculate the normal reaction' or 'Calculate the value of P', worth 2 to 4 marks. The first mark is for a correct resolved component written down; the last is for the value, to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Draw the right-angled triangle, mark the angle, and ask which side of it you want.
